passages.title: Vertical against horizontal scaling
passages.text: A bigger machine or more machines. Scaling up keeps one process and one memory: no coordination, no partitioning, the shortest path for work on one state. It ends at the largest machine you can buy, and one failure takes everything. Scaling out adds instances behind a balancer: capacity grows in steps and a lost instance is one of many, but state must be shared or partitioned and any instance must take any request. The forces: how far the load will grow, whether the work is stateless, what one large machine costs against the ceiling it buys, and what one failure may cost. Scaling up wins for a store that needs transactions over all its data, for a load that fits one machine. Scaling out wins for stateless services, for a load that doubles, and where a failure must be survived. AIW records it as a Chapter 3 decision with both alternatives assessed against the Chapter 2 scalability and availability drivers; the replicas and their zones are Chapter 10 placements, and what one replica carries is a planning assumption on the Chapter 11 desk until a load test replaces it. Ask: what is the ceiling of one machine for this work? Which parts hold state? What happens when the one machine fails?

passages.title: SQL against NoSQL
passages.text: A relational store or a document, key-value, column or graph store. A relational store gives a schema the data must fit, joins across tables and transactions that hold across them; the safer default while the data is still being learnt. A NoSQL store gives a shape per record, partitioning built in and fast reads along one access path; it asks the design to know its queries in advance and to accept weaker guarantees across records. The forces: how many ways the data is read, whether a change must hold across several records, how far the volume will grow, and how well the team knows the store. The relational store wins where the queries are many, where a transaction spans records, and where reporting is expected. The other wins where one access path dominates, where the volume is beyond one machine, and where the shape of a record varies. AIW records it as a Chapter 3 decision with both alternatives assessed against the Chapter 2 integrity and scalability drivers; the store is a Chapter 7 option on the transactional capability; each data definition with its fields, key and classification is a Chapter 8 record. Ask: which queries must the store answer? Which change must hold across records? What is the volume in a year?

passages.title: Batch against stream
passages.text: Work collected and processed at an interval, or processed as each record arrives. Batch processing is simple to reason about, cheap to run and easy to replay: a run has a start, an end and a result that can be checked, as old as the interval. Stream processing gives a result within seconds of the event, at the price of a pipeline that is always on, state kept between events, late and out-of-order records, and harder reprocessing. The forces: how old a result may be, how much the volume varies, whether the consumer acts on each event or on the whole, and what an error costs when it is noticed hours later. Batch wins for reports, reconciliation, billing and anything judged on a complete set. Stream wins for alerts, live views, fraud checks and anything acted on at once. Many designs keep both: a stream for the fast path and a nightly batch that corrects it. AIW records it as a Chapter 3 decision assessed against the Chapter 2 performance and integrity drivers; the processing part is a Chapter 5 component; the hand-over is a Chapter 8 contract of kind event or batch with its data definition. Ask: how old may the answer be? What does a late correction cost? How is a run replayed?

passages.title: Push against pull
passages.text: The producer sends each change to the consumer, or the consumer asks when it wants to know. Push gives the shortest delay and no wasted requests, but the producer must know its consumers, hold what cannot be delivered and cope with a slow or absent one. Pull lets the consumer set its own pace and keeps the producer simple, but a poll that finds nothing is wasted and the delay is the polling interval. The forces: how many consumers there are, how fast a change must reach them, how often changes happen against how often the consumer asks, and which side can be trusted to keep up. Push wins for a few known consumers, for changes that matter at once, and when the producer can buffer. Pull wins for many unknown consumers, for consumers often offline, and when a stale answer is acceptable. AIW records the choice as a Chapter 3 decision assessed against the Chapter 2 performance and recoverability drivers; the exchange is a Chapter 8 contract whose kind and failure policy say which side waits; the Chapter 10 runtime path says whether the dependency is required or buffered. Ask: who must not fall behind? What happens to a change nobody collects? How many consumers will there be?

passages.title: Strong against eventual consistency
passages.text: Every read sees the latest write, or reads may see an older state and converge later. Strong consistency means one truth at any moment: a reader never acts on a stale value, but every write must be agreed before it is confirmed, so writes wait on the slowest replica. Eventual consistency confirms a write locally and spreads it afterwards: fast and available, and able to show two readers two answers. The forces: what a decision on a stale value costs, how far apart the replicas are, how much of the load is reads, and whether the business already tolerates delay. Strong consistency wins for a balance, a stock count, the last seat, and anything a second actor may act on at once. Eventual consistency wins for a timeline, a profile, a catalogue, and anything read far more than written. AIW records the required guarantee as a Chapter 2 integrity driver, the choice as a Chapter 3 decision with its alternatives, and the guarantee each data definition and contract actually gives in Chapter 8, where a duplicate or a stale read becomes a recorded policy. Ask: who acts on this value, and how soon after it changes? What does acting on a stale one cost? Can the business undo a wrong decision?

passages.title: Stateful against stateless
passages.text: A part that keeps something between requests, or a part that keeps nothing and finds what it needs each time. A stateless part can be replaced, restarted and multiplied: any instance answers any request, and a failure loses only the request in flight. It pays with a lookup on every request. A stateful part answers from what it holds, but a request must reach the instance that holds its state, an instance that dies takes its state unless it is replicated, and scaling means moving state. The forces: what the lookup costs, how much state there is, how often the part fails or is replaced, and how the load is spread. Stateless wins for request handlers, workers and anything that must scale or fail over cleanly. Stateful wins for the store itself, for sessions that cannot be externalised, and for a cache close to its reader. AIW records each part's state model as a Chapter 10 plan (stateless process, stateful service or provider managed) with its write authority and protected copy, the component in Chapter 5, and the choice as a Chapter 3 decision when alternatives were weighed. Ask: what does this part hold between two requests? Where does that state live when the instance is gone? Which instance must a request reach?

passages.title: Synchronous against asynchronous
passages.text: The caller waits for the answer, or hands the work over and goes on. A synchronous call is simple to follow; its latency is the sum of every call in the chain, and a slow or absent provider stops the caller with it. An asynchronous hand-over returns as soon as the work is accepted: the caller is shielded from the provider's speed and absence, and the answer arrives later by another path the design must build. The forces: whether the user needs the result to continue, how long the work takes, how reliable the provider is, and what a lost or duplicated message costs. Synchronous wins for a read, a validation, a price, and what the next step needs. Asynchronous wins for work that takes seconds or more, for a provider that is slow or often unavailable, and for a peak that must be absorbed. AIW records the choice as a Chapter 3 decision assessed against the Chapter 2 performance and recoverability drivers; the hand-over is a Chapter 8 contract of kind request or event with its timeout, retry and failure policies and an idempotency key; the Chapter 10 path says whether the dependency is required or buffered. Ask: does the user need the answer now? What happens while the provider is down? How is a duplicate recognised?

passages.title: REST against GraphQL against gRPC
passages.text: Three ways to shape an interface. REST exposes resources over plain HTTP: widely understood and cached by the web; a client that needs several resources makes several calls. GraphQL lets the client state exactly what it wants in one request: fewer round trips and no over-fetching, at the price of a schema to govern, a server that must bound what a query may cost, and caching the web no longer does for free. gRPC sends typed messages over HTTP/2 with generated clients: compact, fast and strict, suited to services talking to services, less so to browsers and to parties without the tooling. The forces: who the callers are, how varied their needs are, how much data a call moves, and how the contract will be versioned. REST wins for public and partner interfaces. GraphQL wins for a client-driven product with many screens over one data model. gRPC wins between internal services on a hot path. AIW records the choice as a Chapter 3 decision assessed against the Chapter 2 performance and interoperability drivers; each interface is a Chapter 8 contract with its protocol, operation, version and payload; the framework is a Chapter 7 option. Ask: who calls this, and with what tooling? How will the contract change without breaking them? What does a call move?

passages.title: Long polling against WebSockets against server-sent events
passages.text: Three ways for a server to reach a browser. Long polling holds an ordinary request open until there is news: it works everywhere, but every message costs a request and the gap between them is silence. Server-sent events keep one HTTP response open and stream events down it: simple and proxied like HTTP, but one direction and text only. WebSockets open a two-way channel either side may write to: the lowest latency, at the price of a stateful connection the server must hold, scale and recover. The forces: whether the client must also send, how many connections the server holds at once, how long a message may wait, and what the network allows. Long polling wins for rare updates behind strict networks. Server-sent events win for a feed, a status page, a progress bar. WebSockets win for chat, collaboration and anything where both sides talk often. AIW records it as a Chapter 3 decision assessed against the Chapter 2 performance and scalability drivers; the channel is a Chapter 8 contract with its protocol; the connections a server holds and how they survive a restart are a Chapter 10 plan's state model and capacity basis. Ask: must the client send as well as receive? How many open connections at peak? What happens to them when an instance restarts?

passages.title: Read-through against write-through against write-back caching
passages.text: Where the cache sits in the path of a read and a write. Read-through fills the cache on a miss: the first reader pays, the next are fast, and a value can be stale until it expires. Write-through writes to the cache and the store together: reads are fresh and a restart loses nothing, but every write pays twice and the cache fills with values nobody reads. Write-back writes to the cache and to the store later: the fastest writes, at the price of data that exists only in memory until it is flushed, which a crash loses. The forces: the ratio of reads to writes, how stale a read may be, what a lost write costs. Read-through wins for read-heavy data. Write-through wins where a read after a write must be fresh and writes are modest. Write-back wins for counters, metrics and anything that can be rebuilt. AIW records the caching need as a Chapter 6 capability and the product as a Chapter 7 option; the choice is a Chapter 3 decision assessed against the Chapter 2 performance and integrity drivers; the Chapter 8 data definition says who is authoritative, which the cache never is. Ask: how stale may a read be? What is lost if the cache is lost? What share of reads hits?

passages.title: Normalisation against denormalisation
passages.text: Each fact kept once and joined when read, or facts copied to where they are read. A normalised model has one place for each fact, so an update is one write and nothing can disagree; a read that needs several facts joins several tables. A denormalised model keeps the facts a reader needs together: a read is one lookup, but an update must reach every copy, copies can disagree in between, and the model is shaped by today's reads. The forces: the ratio of reads to writes, how many access paths there are, what a disagreement between copies costs, and whether the store can join at all. Normalisation wins for data that changes often, is read in many ways, and must never disagree with itself. Denormalisation wins for read-heavy paths with a known shape, for stores that do not join, and for reports. Most designs normalise the source, denormalise a view of it. AIW records each data definition, its fields and its authority in Chapter 8, a copy as lineage between two definitions, and the choice as a Chapter 3 decision assessed against the Chapter 2 integrity and performance drivers. Ask: which definition is the source of truth? How does a change reach each copy, and how long may they disagree? Which reads justify a copy?

passages.title: Latency against throughput
passages.text: How long one request takes, or how many requests complete in a second. The two are different targets and pull against each other: batching, queueing and larger buffers raise throughput by making each request wait a little; dedicated resources and short paths cut latency by leaving capacity idle. A system near its capacity gives its worst latency. The forces: whether a person is waiting on the request, whether the work arrives in bursts or steadily, what an idle replica costs against what a slow second costs, and whether the work can be grouped. Latency wins for anything a person waits on. Throughput wins for pipelines, imports, reconciliation and the work behind a queue, where the measure is the backlog cleared, not the wait of one item. AIW records each as a Chapter 2 driver with a numeric target, a window and a measurement: a percentile in milliseconds for latency, a rate at a peak for throughput; the replicas that carry the rate are Chapter 10 placements, and the Chapter 11 desk turns the objective into requests a second, replicas and a time budget per hop, each number with its assumption. Ask: who waits on this, and at what percentile? What is the peak rate, not the average? At what utilisation will it run?

passages.title: Availability against consistency under partition
passages.text: When the replicas cannot reach each other, a system must choose: keep answering and risk two answers, or refuse until the replicas agree. A system that stays available serves each side from what it has, so two writers may both succeed. A system that stays consistent stops the side that cannot reach a majority, so some callers get an error. The forces: what a conflicting write costs against what a refused request costs, how long a partition may last, whether the business can reconcile afterwards, and which operations must never disagree. Availability wins for reads, for anything a person can retry and the business can merge. Consistency wins for money, stock, bookings and identity, where two truths are worse than a pause. The choice is per operation, not per system. AIW records the required behaviour as a Chapter 2 availability or integrity driver, the choice as a Chapter 3 decision with both alternatives assessed against those drivers, what each contract does when the other side is unreachable as its Chapter 8 failure policy, and the recovery strategy and failure domains as Chapter 10 plans and zones. Ask: for each operation, is a wrong answer or no answer worse? How are conflicting writes found and merged? How long can the business wait?

passages.title: Monolith against modular monolith against microservices
passages.text: One deployable with one code base, one deployable with enforced internal boundaries, or many deployables each owning a boundary. A monolith is the simplest: It grows until every change touches everything. A modular monolith keeps the one deployable but draws the boundaries inside it, so each module owns its data and declares its interfaces; it costs discipline, not infrastructure. Microservices turn those boundaries into separate deployables that scale, fail and release independently, at the price of a network between every call, no transaction across the whole. The forces: the size and number of teams, how differently the parts must scale or change, and how well the boundaries are understood. The monolith wins for a small team and a product still finding its shape. The modular monolith wins for most teams for most of a product's life. Microservices win where teams must release independently and loads differ, and only when the boundaries are known. AIW records the responsibilities and their boundaries in Chapter 4, the components in Chapter 5, the style as a Chapter 3 decision assessed against the Chapter 2 maintainability, scalability and deployability drivers, and each deployable's plan in Chapter 10. Ask: how many teams, and how do they release? Which boundaries are certain? What does a network call add to each step?

passages.title: Build against buy against SaaS
passages.text: Write the capability, license a product and run it, or subscribe to a service someone else runs. Building gives exactly what the design needs and keeps every change in the team's hands, at the full cost of writing, operating and securing it. Buying gives a mature capability the team still runs: patched, sized and backed up. A service gives the capability with none of the running, at the price of a dependency outside the design: its availability, data location and price are the provider's, and leaving it is a project. The forces: whether the capability differentiates the product, what it costs to operate well, what data in it may not leave, and how far the provider may be trusted. Build wins for the capability that is the product. Buy wins for a capability that must run inside the boundary. A service wins for commodity capabilities, and where the provider's scale is the point. AIW records the capability in Chapter 6, the options compared in Chapter 7, the decision in Chapter 3 against the Chapter 2 drivers and the constraints, and a service as a Chapter 8 party with the contracts that reach it, their timeouts and failure policies. Ask: does this capability make the product different? Where may its data live? What does leaving cost in a year?

figures.title: L1 cache reference
figures.text: About half a nanosecond: the fastest memory a processor has, so work that stays in it costs nothing a design can see.

figures.title: Main memory reference
figures.text: About a hundred nanoseconds, two hundred times an L1 hit: a structure that does not fit the cache is read at this speed.

figures.title: Compress 1 KB
figures.text: About ten microseconds with a fast compressor: compressing a payload costs far less than sending it across a data centre.

figures.title: Read 4 KB at random from an SSD
figures.text: About 150 microseconds: a random SSD read is a thousand times a memory reference and a hundred times cheaper than a disk seek.

figures.title: Read 1 MB sequentially from memory
figures.text: About a quarter of a millisecond: scanning a megabyte in memory is cheap next to any network hop.

figures.title: Round trip inside one data centre
figures.text: About half a millisecond: every synchronous call between two parts in one data centre spends at least this on the network.

figures.title: Read 1 MB sequentially from an SSD
figures.text: About a millisecond: four times the memory scan, and twice the data-centre round trip.

figures.title: Disk seek
figures.text: About ten milliseconds: a spinning disk's seek is the slowest step inside a machine, so random reads from disk set the floor for anything that depends on them.

figures.title: Round trip across a region
figures.text: About ten milliseconds for data centres a thousand kilometres apart: light in fibre covers about 200 kilometres a millisecond, there and back, before any switch adds its own.

figures.title: Read 1 MB sequentially from disk
figures.text: About twenty milliseconds: twenty times the SSD scan and eighty times the memory scan.

figures.title: Round trip across the world
figures.text: About 150 milliseconds between continents: a synchronous call across the world spends most of a sub-second budget on the network alone.

figuresNote: Reference orders of magnitude for estimation, not measurements of any system: the values follow the widely circulated list of latency figures the attributed source reproduces, rounded; measure before relying on one.
